passages.title: Why board games are back
passages.text:
On a rainy Tuesday evening, every table at The Dice Box in Manchester is full. Groups of friends are laughing, arguing and rolling dice, and hardly anyone is looking at a phone. (1) ________ Today there are more than five hundred across the country.

Customers pay £6 each to sit at a table for as long as they like, and they can choose from a library of over 800 games. (2) ________ That is why the café employs 'game guides', staff whose job is to recommend a game and explain the rules.

The owner, Tom Bradley, opened the café in 2019 after losing his job at a bank. He believes the reason for its success is simple. 'People spend all day looking at a computer at work,' he says. (3) ________ 'A screen can never give them that.'

The customers are not only young people. On Sunday afternoons the café is full of families, and a group of retired teachers meets there every Thursday morning. (4) ________ 'I play against my grandchildren now, and I usually win,' she laughs.

Running a games café is not always easy, though. New games are expensive, and small pieces often go missing. (5) ________ It takes time, but Tom says it is worth it. 'A game with one card missing is a game nobody can finish.'

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (1)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'Places like this' refers to The Dice Box, and 'Ten years ago, however' contrasts with the next sentence: 'Today there are more than five hundred across the country.' The sentence saying most customers prefer to play on their phones contradicts 'hardly anyone is looking at a phone'.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (2)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'So many on the shelves' refers to 'a library of over 800 games', and the problem that 'newcomers often have no idea where to start' explains the next sentence: 'That is why the café employs game guides… to recommend a game.' The sentence about the café stopping buying games has no cause here and does not lead to game guides.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (3)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'They' refers to the 'People' who spend 'all day looking at a computer at work', and sitting 'round a real table with real people' is what 'that' means in Tom's next words: 'A screen can never give them that.' The sentence about Tom learning chess does not continue his quote and gives 'that' nothing to refer to.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (4)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'One of them' refers to the 'group of retired teachers', and introducing Margaret explains who 'she' is in the next sentence: 'I play against my grandchildren now… she laughs.' The sentence about Tom learning chess cannot fit, because the next speaker is a woman with grandchildren.

questions.question: Which sentence fits gap (5)?
options: A) To stop this happening, staff check that every box is complete after it has been used.
B) In the evening, they want to sit round a real table with real people.
C) Ten years ago, however, places like this were very hard to find in Britain.
D) Most customers prefer to play games on their phones while they wait for their food.
E) One of them, 72-year-old Margaret Lowe, says the games keep her mind sharp.
F) Tom himself learnt to play chess from his grandfather when he was five.
G) As a result, the café has decided to stop buying new games.
H) With so many on the shelves, newcomers often have no idea where to start.
questions.explanation: 'To stop this happening' refers to 'small pieces often go missing', and checking every box is what 'It takes time' describes; Tom adds that 'A game with one card missing is a game nobody can finish.' The sentence about stopping buying new games does not explain what 'takes time' or why a missing card matters.
